The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Investment memo · Arteche Lantegi Elkartea (ART-ES)

Arteche (ART-ES) is a better business than its share price: worth owning, but not at 23 times earnings, and the entry point comes after the March 2027 guidance

Written 1-Nov-2026 for Richard. Price €31.3 (28-Oct-2026); 58.1m shares; market capitalisation about €1.83bn; enterprise value about €1.9bn. All money is in euros. The forecasts, consensus and bases used are defined in the end notes.

#0Summary: the business, the case, and what matters

Arteche's business is better than its share price is likely to be over the next twelve months. Want the stock, but buy it after the market has re-priced it, not at today's multiple.

Arteche is a top-two global maker of high-voltage instrument transformers, and it is winning more than its share of the strongest grid-equipment demand in a generation. Arteche holds about 15% of the global market and 20% to 30% of the US market, leads the world in auxiliary relays, runs 13 plants on four continents, and is homologated (formally qualified as a supplier) with about 90% of the world's utilities after 80 years of engineering. Arteche gains share because it can deliver while the Tier-1 makers quote lead times of three to five years.

Arteche's balance sheet is lightly geared (net debt 0.5x EBITDA). The founding family controls the company with allied shareholders but has begun to widen the shareholder register. Arteche's strategy (capacity built ahead of demand, leadership in SF6-free products that avoid the greenhouse gas sulphur hexafluoride, and a push into protection and automation through the acquired SEG Electronics) is coherent and well funded.

Six conclusions drive the case.

1The demand force is real, funded and dated, and demand is not the risk. Spain's €17.9bn grid decree, the US exclusion of vendors tied to 24 countries from equipment of 69 kV and above (instrument transformers are named; the rules are due 24-Dec-2026), the EU's F-gas phase-out and Brazil's distribution plan all arrived in the last six months. Volume growth of 8% to 10% a year for four years is the high-confidence part of the forecast.
2The margin step has already happened, and price drove it, not operating leverage. From FY2022 to H1 2026 the direct margin rose 11.2 points and the EBITDA margin 10.9 points, so overheads contributed nothing net. Arteche's backlog turns over in nine months, so no tail of old low-priced contracts is left to roll off; from FY2027 the margin can rise only through overhead re-absorption and mix. The model holds the EBITDA margin on a plateau of 18.0% to 18.6%; consensus has 18.9% in FY2028, and one broker has 21.3% in FY2029. The margin path is the largest disagreement with the market, and it decides the multiple.
3FY2026 is safe; FY2027 consensus EPS is too high because of the lines below EBIT. Our FY2027 EPS after minorities is €1.22, against a consensus median of €1.40 and a mean of €1.33. Most of the gap comes from lines that nobody guides and that the two domestic brokers model inconsistently: tax normalising from 14% toward 20%, net financial items of about €9m that the FactSet median nearly omits, minorities, and the amortisation of the SEG acquisition. The operating gap is small.
4Arteche's guidance habit produces a dated negative event in March 2027. Management sets guidance low and raises it at the half-year. Applying that pattern to FY2026 actuals, the first FY2027 guidance (24-Mar-2027) will most likely read about €112m to €120m of EBITDA, 5% to 10% below consensus. "Guidance below consensus from a company that never misses" is the most probable headline of the next six months, and that headline is the moment consensus moves toward our numbers.
5The risk sits in the share price, not in the business. Arteche's two-year-forward P/E is 23.4x on our earnings (19.8x on consensus), at the 91st percentile of its ten-year history. Arteche's closest fundamental analogue, Pfisterer, trades at 14.1x, at the 0th percentile of its history, after a 48% fall on an order normalisation. Arteche carries every marker of the Pfisterer pattern (a recent listing, a thin float with more secondary supply planned, two domestic brokers at 100% buy, a multiple built by its own re-rating) except the trigger. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 17.67x is 25% below today's, and at 17.67x the model's total shareholder return is −11% to end-2027 and roughly nil to mid-2029.
6The constructive angle is timing, not stance. Arteche is a business Richard would want to own at the right multiple. The next six months carry a queue of events more likely to compress the multiple than to expand it: Pfisterer's third-quarter results (18-Nov), the Spanish election (29-Nov), the first FY2027 guidance (March) and a family share placement toward a 20% to 25% float. After that queue, a guidance raise at the H1 2027 results (about 60% likely) restarts the beat-and-raise cycle from a lower base. The entry point the case wants is probably in 2027, at 14x to 17x earnings, once the market has learned how Arteche guides.

Five judgements move the shares most; each is sized below

The base for the arithmetic is FY2027 of record: revenue €659.6m, EBITDA €121.4m (18.4%), pre-tax profit €90.9m, tax at 19%, minorities €2.7m, 58.05m shares, and EPS of €1.22 after minorities (€1.27 in the model, which omits minorities). Three rules of thumb follow: each 1% of price is worth about 0.8 point of EBITDA margin; the contribution margin on extra volume is about 40%; each point of tax rate is worth about €0.9m of profit.

Judgement 1: the direct margin (price minus input costs, plus mix) holds near 40% through FY2028. Each point of direct margin is worth €6.6m of EBITDA, €5.3m of profit after 19% tax, €0.09 a share and 7.5% of FY2027 EPS. The downside the sector's history argues for is new-order prices falling 2% from 2028 as Tier-1, Korean and Chinese capacity arrives; that fall would cost the FY2028 EBITDA margin about 1.6 points. A cost shock like 2021-22's, not passed through for a year, would cut the direct margin by about 3 points in the year it hits. The upside is overhead growth held to 7% a year on the consensus revenue path.

Judgement 2: the new capacity converts the backlog on schedule. The FY2027 revenue forecast is a forecast of the capacity ramp, not of demand. Each 5% of FY2027 revenue (€33m) at a 40% drop-through is worth €13m of EBITDA, €10.7m of profit after tax and €0.18 a share (±15% of EPS). The model's downside case (ramp delays plus Latin American order timing) gives revenue of €621m and EPS of €0.98; the model's upside case gives €684m and €1.37. For FY2026 the same arithmetic values the gap between consensus H2 revenue of €311m (+21%) and our €299m (+16%) at €5m of EBITDA and €0.07 of EPS: material to the headline, not to the thesis.

Judgement 3: the lines below EBIT normalise, and they alone explain the gap to consensus FY2027 EPS. Net financial items of €9m, against the roughly €1m the FactSet FY2027 median implies, cost €8m pre-tax, €6.5m after tax and €0.11 a share. A 19% tax rate, against Santander's flat 16%, costs 3 points on €90.9m of pre-tax profit: €2.7m, or €0.05 a share. Minorities of €2.7m cost another €0.05. Together these three lines take about €0.20 a share, enough on their own to explain the gap between our €1.22 and the median €1.40 before any operating disagreement. If Bizkaia's new 19% minimum effective tax rate and the mix shift toward Mexico, Brazil and Germany push the group tax rate to 22% a year earlier than we model, FY2027 EPS loses another €0.05.

Judgement 4: the multiple the market will pay for a margin plateau is the biggest lever, and its distribution is skewed down. At end-2027 the model's forward earnings base is FY2029 EPS of €1.52 (€1.47 after minorities), so each turn of the P/E multiple is worth €1.52 a share, or 4.8% of today's price. Holding today's 23.4x gives a return of +17% including about €1.0 of dividends; 20x roughly breaks even; the guideline 17.67x gives −11%; the small-cap grid cohort's 14x (Pfisterer's multiple today) gives −29%; the stock's ten-year median of 13.6x gives −31%. The multiple moves the shares more than any operating judgement.

Judgement 5: the ambition of the Strategic Plan 2030, and the capital it deploys, can lift the path. A plan at our path (2030 revenue about €860m, margin 18.3%, EPS €1.57) validates the model and disappoints the bull broker. A plan at €950m of revenue and a 21% margin implies 2030 EBITDA of about €200m, €43m above ours and worth about €0.58 of EPS after 22% tax; FY2030 EPS would be about €2.1 (+35% on ours), a path that would hold today's multiple. Separately, each €100m of debt-funded bolt-on acquisitions at SEG's price (about 10x EBITDA) adds about €10m of EBITDA and €4.3m of profit after interest and tax: +€0.07 a share, or 5% to 7% of EPS. Arteche's balance sheet carries €150m to €250m of such capacity by FY2028, so one more SEG-sized deal within 18 months is likely, and no such deal is in the base case.

Scorecard

#1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Judgement: Arteche's external forces are among the strongest of any European industrial for the next 18 to 24 months, and in the last six months they moved from planned to legally authorised and funded. The headwinds are real but sit elsewhere: in the discount rate and sector positioning now, and in industry capacity from 2027 to 2029. Demand is not what will go wrong.

Evidence: the demand case moved from forecasts to law. Until the last six months the demand case rested on forecasts: a record $1.7 trillion of global grid investment in 2026, the EU's €580bn by 2030, and US utilities' $1.3 to $1.4 trillion over five years. The last six months added dated law aimed at Arteche's products, summarised in the table below. Three details matter beyond the headline sums. Spain's Royal Decree 640/2026 lifts the caps that tied grid investment to GDP and earmarks 20% of the distribution budget for voltage control and remote management. Spain's €615m grid-resilience package, a response to the April 2025 Iberian blackout, includes about €366m for electronic compensators and €143m for shunt reactors, alongside a separate €9bn, ten-year capacity market. In the US, the Defense Production Act determinations of April 2026 named transformers, substations and protective relays as critical, before the late-August executive order fenced out vendors from 24 countries.

Arteche's own exposure is direct: over 35% of revenue is tied to integrating renewables into the grid, and Arteche launched the first 400 kV SF6-free instrument transformer.

Inference: two forces are layered, and the price force fades first. The structural force (electrification, renewables, replacement of 30- to 40-year-old assets, and data-centre connections) drives the served market's volume at roughly 7% to 10% a year in value, and Arteche's share gains add 2 to 4 points on top while Tier-1 order books run at $50bn to $60bn. The cyclical force (scarcity: power-transformer lead times of 2.5 to 4.5 years and prices up 81% since 2021) drives price, and price is the part that fades first. The regulatory fences work differently from either force: the US executive order lowers competitive intensity in Arteche's largest single market for years, and SF6-free re-qualification resets the competitive field in favour of incumbents with new products.

So what: the volume forecast (8% to 10% organic growth a year to FY2030) deserves high confidence and is the foundation of the earnings case. The price forecast (+3.5% in FY2026, fading to nil by FY2029) is where the model has already taken the fade; the market has not.

The headwinds, weighed honestly, hit timing and price rather than demand.

(a) Spain converts slowly:only 12% of grid-access requests were approved in 2025, 86.5% of substations are saturated, the 2025-30 network plan still lacks its environmental assessment, and the snap election of 29-Nov-2026 will push the plan of Redeia (the Spanish grid operator) into late 2027. One expert sizes Spain's programme at only €30m to €80m of cumulative orders for Arteche through 2030. Spain is a slow, modest tailwind, not the transformational one the domestic press describes.
(b) The capacity wave arrives from 2027:Siemens Energy is adding 50% to its transformer and switchgear capacity by 2030; Hitachi Energy is building a $528m plant in Mississippi (2029); GE Vernova's Charleroi expansion includes instrument transformers (2028); Ritz's 765 kV plant is open; Pfiffner's 550 kV plant opens in 2027; Quality Power's Mehru plant is moving to 500 kV; and India's transformer capacity is nearly doubling. Morgan Stanley, Jefferies and Rothschild & Co Redburn all place the pricing peak in 2026-27 and the decline from 2028-29.
(c) Macro conditions punish the sector:the US 10-year yield is near 5.1%, Brent oil is at $111, and European defensive stocks are leading; in October 2026 the sector's leaders fell 12% to 20% while their orders rose.
(d) Currency translation is unhedged:about 49% of revenue is in currencies other than the euro, and translating it cost €16.5m through equity in H1 2026; transaction exposure is hedged over short horizons.
(e) US trade rules are tightening:Section 301 duties of 10% apply to Spanish-made exports; the 15% Section 232 rate on grid equipment expires on 31-Dec-2027; and the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) moves to annual reviews from 2027, with October guidance tying reduced duties to 85% US-melted metal content, so Arteche's route to the US through its Tepeji del Río plant in Mexico is now reviewed every year.

Strongest counter-case. The growth rate of grid spending may peak in 2026 (Morgan Stanley's peak of 6%; US utility capital spending growth slowing to 5% in 2027), and capital-goods share prices turn on the rate of change of order growth, not on its level. If so, the external picture is already as good as it gets for the shares, even as it keeps improving for revenue. I think that counter-case is right, and it is why this topic scores high for the business while the later topics score low for the stock.

What would change my view. Constant-currency order growth below 10% for two halves, or a book-to-bill ratio below 1.05; a Department of Energy rule that makes Mexican assembly conditional on US content. Spain's plan slipping beyond 2027 would hit FY2028 volume, not FY2027 volume.

Versus the market. We agree with the market on demand. We differ on what demand buys: the market reads the backlog as visibility and the Spanish decree as a near-term catalyst; we read the backlog as a conversion constraint and Spain as late-2027 volume, at discounted prices, for the qualified majors.

78

Score: 78. Funded, dated, product-specific mandates in three regions plus a US regulatory fence put Arteche near the top of European industrials on tailwinds; the capacity wave of 2027-29 and the sector's discount-rate sensitivity keep it out of the top decile.

#2Internally driven corporate change, and the absence of problems

Judgement: management is executing a broad, well-resourced growth programme (capacity doubled, three acquisitions in a year, a main-market listing, the payout doubled, guidance raised), and the changes fit the external forces. The changes are a response to the cycle rather than a transformation, and there is no new chief executive. The changes share one cost: overheads, working capital and management bandwidth are being consumed faster than revenue grows. The internal story therefore moves the forecasting risk from demand to conversion.

Evidence of positive change: Arteche is investing on every front at once. Capital spending doubles to about €40m in FY2026, of which €34m to €35m goes to capacity, automation and innovation. About €72m went on acquisitions and stakes in twelve months, at sensible prices. FY2026 guidance was raised at every line on 28-Jul-2026, and the 2024-26 plan (2026 revenue of €520m to €540m, margin of 12.5% to 13%) was beaten by 8% on revenue and 500 basis points on margin a year early.

Evidence of the cost: overheads, working capital and supplier finance are all rising faster than revenue. The direct margin rose about 380 basis points from FY2025 to H1 2026 but the EBITDA margin rose only 260, so overheads absorbed about 120 basis points as new plants, SEG, listing costs and a €4.5m long-term incentive accrual landed ahead of volume. Inventories rose from €84m to €108m in six months. Non-recourse factoring reached €12.4m alongside the reverse factoring shown below. Free cash flow in FY2026 (about €14m to €18m) is below the €22.6m dividend paid in May. Capitalised development not yet certified doubled to €5.3m. SEG's €47.4m of provisional goodwill sits on €3.2m of net assets, with no synergy targets; SEG's pro-forma disclosure (net profit only €0.66m higher with SEG consolidated from 1-Jan) implies that SEG's first half ran well below the "above 20%" margin its seller, Aurelius, advertised. The family sold about €67m of stock in June and intends to lift the free float, now about 20%, into a range of 20% to 25%.

Inference: Arteche's internal forces are strong on delivery and ordinary on capital allocation. Arteche is run by a family steward-operator that grows aggressively within its niches, buys sensibly (SEG at roughly 8x to 13x EBITDA, against listed peers at 16x to 20x), raised €33m of new equity at €33 a share near the top of its own price range, and has never bought back a share. The strategic pivot toward automation moves Arteche toward higher-margin profit pools (automation EBIT margins of 15% to 23.5%), but also into territory where Siemens, ABB, Schneider and GE Vernova bundle software with hardware, which is exactly where the "small specialist versus giant" test warns a small company to be careful.

So what: the model carries the cost of growth explicitly, on lines the sell-side does not discuss. The model has structural costs at 23.5% of income in FY2026, falling to 22.4% by FY2028 only because revenue grows 10% or more; working capital at 19% of revenue; capital spending at €43m to €45m; and depreciation rising €8.6m by FY2028. Two steps can disappoint on these lines: the step from revenue to EBITDA (do overheads re-absorb?) and the step from EBITDA to cash (does working capital normalise?).

Strongest counter-case. The overhead build is exactly what a company should do in a supply-short market; the precedent of Hammond (a 140 basis-point drag during its plant ramp, recovered within three quarters) shows that ramps pay back quickly; and management's record earns the benefit of the doubt. I agree on the first two points. On the third, the 2021-22 episode matters, because the same team delivered revenue then and lost 340 basis points of margin when input costs rose.

What would change my view. Structural costs at or below 22.5% of income in H1 2027 (re-absorption ahead of plan); working capital at or below 19% of revenue at end-2026 with reverse factoring flat; a formal separation of the chair and chief-executive roles; a Strategic Plan 2030 that quantifies SEG synergies and sets a return-on-capital target.

Versus the market. The market sees the acquisitions as margin-accretive from day one and the new capacity as pure upside. We see the acquisitions and the capacity as right but dilutive to returns in FY2026-27, and we model SEG at a 17% to 20% margin rather than above 20%.

64

Score: 64. A broad, funded and congruent programme with a strong delivery record ranks Arteche well above the median European industrial; the absence of a transformation lever, the overhead and working-capital build, and family-first governance at regulatory minimums keep it out of the top quartile.

#3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Judgement: Arteche's niche (high-voltage equipment gated by utility homologation, concentrated among margin-first incumbents, with customers who buy on delivery certainty) is about as favourable an industry structure as capital goods offers. Arteche's moat protects its volume and share durably, but not its price. Arteche's financial profile is above average on growth, margins, returns and leverage and below average on cash conversion. Management is a capable, delivery-focused operator with a strong record, and its governance is below peers'.

Value chain and structure: strong customers, disciplined competitors and stronger suppliers.

  • Customers are strong and committed. Utilities supply 30% of revenue, distributors 25%, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors 20% and original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) 15%. Customers sign multi-year frame agreements, and Red Eléctrica ranks technical compliance and qualification first, delivery certainty second and price third.
  • Competitors are disciplined. Hitachi Energy and Mitsubishi put margin ahead of share, and Hitachi partners with Arteche (through AGIT) rather than fighting it. Five makers plausibly hold more than half of the high-voltage instrument-transformer market: Trench, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, Arteche, and one of Pfiffner, Ritz, Končar or a Chinese maker.
  • Suppliers have gained power. Grain-oriented steel comes from very few mills; copper is up 40%; Spain's prompt-payment law has compressed days payable from 87 to 73; cast-resin parts and relay modules are single-sourced.
  • The structure's fragility is dated and visible. Tier-1 and Asian capacity arrives from 2027 to 2029. Chinese makers deliver 95% to 98% of Western quality at 60% to 80% of the cost, and are redirecting supply to Europe and Latin America as the US fences them out. Tier-1 software bundling works against Arteche's automation ambition.
One structural event in the last week matters: GE Vernova agreed on 28-Oct-2026 to buy Trench, the instrument-transformer leader, for about $9bn (13x 2028 EBITDA and 18x 2026 EBITDA, on a projected 37% EBITDA margin).

The Trench deal puts the niche leader inside a Tier-1 maker and gives a private-market valuation reference. The deal may also push Hitachi Energy and Siemens Energy, which now buy bushings and instrument transformers from a direct competitor, toward neutral suppliers, which for Arteche means AGIT and its own product lines. Bernstein calls that conflict overblown, so the shift of volume to Arteche is a tail outcome, not the base case.

Business model and competitive advantage: two kinds of advantage must be kept apart. Arteche's barriers against new entrants are strong and widening: homologation takes two to five years per utility across more than 1,500 utilities, and Arteche has the US fence, SF6-free re-qualification and USMCA-compliant Mexican production on its side. Arteche's advantages over existing rivals (delivery capacity, customisation, speed and in-house test laboratories) are real but rest on execution and are time-limited; in the words of one source, "the early-mover window is not a moat". Against the Tier-1 makers, who hold equivalent homologations, Arteche's edge is agility, not cost or scale; management itself says Arteche cannot compete with Hitachi or Siemens on low-cost products made in India or China. Arteche is small in absolute terms (€535m of revenue over the last twelve months, against Siemens Energy's €45bn) but large enough within its niche. Arteche has no network effect and no evidence of sharing scale economies with customers. Arteche prices to scarcity, so customers will owe it no goodwill on price when supply normalises.

Financial profile: above average on growth, margins, returns and leverage; weak on cash. Revenue compounded at 12.2% a year over FY2019-25. Arteche's post-tax return on capital employed is roughly 18% to 21% including intangibles and above 35% on tangible capital (our arithmetic; the company does not disclose it). Net financial debt is 0.5x EBITDA, interest cover is above 15x, and 79% of loans are fixed at 3.6%. Cash is the weak link: FactSet free cash flow fell from 178% of net income in FY2023 to 58% in FY2025, and the model has 0.3x to 0.4x in FY2026-27 before a recovery to 0.6x to 0.75x. Two items flatter the reported numbers: the FY2025 tax rate of 14.2% (worth €0.07 to €0.08 of the €0.79 EPS), and about €7m a year of capitalised development inside EBITDA (about 1 point of margin that peers such as Landis+Gyr expense).

Management: a capable, stable, engineering-led team, with governance below peers. Alexander Artetxe (third generation of the family, Chairman and long the chief executive) restructured the balance sheet in 2017, built the Mexican business, took the company from the BME Growth junior market (share price €3.94 in 2021) to the main market, delivered two plans early and bought sensibly. The team (chief executive Pérez, chief financial officer Vicente and chief business officer Fernández) is stable, engineering-led and Spain-centred, with an average tenure of nine years. Communication is clear within a thin format: reporting is half-yearly only, with no quarterly numbers and no disclosure below EBITDA or on SEG. Governance lags peers: 36% of directors are independent, against 75% to 89% at Prysmian and GE Vernova; insiders hold four of five seats on the Strategy Commission; the chair and chief-executive roles stay combined until the split is confirmed; directors received a €726k listing bonus; there have been no buybacks; and the payout policy coincides with the family's interest in liquidity. Ambition is substantial relative to Arteche's past (€800m to €900m of 2030 revenue) and moderate relative to Pfisterer, which is tripling its Czech capacity.

So what: forecast Arteche's volume with high confidence and its price with low confidence, which is the shape of the model. Expect management to deliver what it guides and to under-disclose what it does not guide. Expect returns on capital to dilute in FY2026-27 as goodwill and plants built ahead of volume enter the capital base.

Strongest counter-case. The moat may protect price more than I allow. Pfisterer's gross margin followed the same path (38.5% to 41.8%, now stabilising), and Trench's 37% EBITDA margin shows what the niche earns at scale; if today's margin level belongs to the niche rather than to the cycle, the margin plateau is a floor, not a ceiling. This is the best bull argument in the file, and it is why the base case holds the margin at 18% to 18.6% rather than letting it revert toward the single digits of 2019-22.

What would change my view. Evidence of share loss in high-voltage measurement (none today); a price war in instrument transformers led by a Tier-1 maker (improbable while all are sold out); a formal split of the chair and chief-executive roles and a return-on-capital target (either would raise the management score).

Versus the market. We agree with the market on the quality of the franchise. We differ on cash conversion, which the market does not discuss, and on governance, which the domestic brokers do not score.

66

Score: 66. A top-two position in a homologation-gated niche with above-average growth, margins, returns and balance sheet puts Arteche well above the European median; cash conversion in the bottom quartile, a non-scale cost position and governance at regulatory minimums keep it below the top quartile.

#4Conservative guidance; keeping the sell-side conservative; the record of delivery and upgrades

Judgement: Arteche is a precise sandbagger. Management sets guidance low, beats the top of the range, raises at the half-year and resets at plan events, and the record is unbroken for four years. But management has not kept the sell-side conservative: consensus already sits above the top of the EBITDA range and at the top of the revenue range, and informal commentary runs above formal guidance. Arteche's record therefore guarantees a beat against guidance, not a beat against expectations.

Evidence: guidance is low, beaten every year, and already exceeded by consensus. FY2026 guidance, raised on 28-Jul-2026, is revenue of €565m to €590m and EBITDA of €92.1m to €100.4m (16.3% to 17.8% margin), up from €555m to €585m and €87.7m to €95.4m. The top of the EBITDA range implies an H2 margin of only 15.8%: flat on H2 2025 and 260 basis points below H1 2026, although H2 has not been below H1 in any of the last three years. Arteche's EBITDA beat the top of its range by 0.3% in FY2022, rising to 4.4% in FY2025 (€78m against €72.5m to €77m, on the Spanish accounting basis). Consensus has FY2026 revenue of €589m (the top of the range) and EBITDA of €105m (4.6% above the top, and about 6% above on a like-for-like basis, because the brokers' basis ran 1.7% below IFRS last year). Over twelve months FY2027 consensus EPS rose 34% and EBITDA 27% while sales rose only 7%, so the upgrades were led by margin. Guidance covers only EBITDA and only FY2026, and there are no mid-term targets until the Strategic Plan 2030. Arteche's one historical miss came in the 2020-23 plan, which beat revenue heavily (11.9% organic growth a year against 4.5%) but missed the direct margin by 248 basis points in the 2021-22 inflation.

Inference: three consequences follow from the pattern.

  1. The FY2026 beat is already in consensus. FY2026 EBITDA above €100.4m is about 80% likely (we forecast €103.7m), and €106m or more is plausible if H2 holds the H1 margin. But consensus is already €105m, so the visible beat against expectations is €0m to €2m, not €5m.
  2. The pattern will produce a negative event. FY2026's first range assumed revenue growth of 9% to 15% and a flat margin. Applied to FY2026 actuals, the same pattern gives FY2027 revenue of €628m to €663m and EBITDA of €112m to €120m, against consensus of €683m and €126m (Santander €135m).
  3. The Strategic Plan 2030 will be set the way the last plan was. The last plan assumed 10% compound growth and 250 basis points of margin gain, and was beaten by a wide margin. 2030 ambitions of €845m to €910m of revenue and an 18% to 20% margin are therefore the base case, with about a 25% chance of something near the bull broker's €950m and 21%.
So what: Arteche's track record lowers delivery risk (the FY2026 cone is ±4% on EBITDA) but is a liability for the near-term narrative, because the market has priced the record as "beat-and-raise forever" rather than "guide low, then beat". The question for the next 12 months is whether the market has learned the pattern; stalled revisions and a 100% buy share say the market has not fully learned it.

Strongest counter-case. Management may break the pattern at the plan and give FY2027 guidance that brackets consensus (about 25% likely), or a strong H2 2026 (margin at or above 18.4%) may lift the FY2026 base enough that even a cautious FY2027 range reads well. Both are possible; the H2 2026 margin is the swing factor.

What would change my view. A nine-month trading update with a backlog at or above €420m and order growth at or above 10% in constant currency (which would keep FY2027 inside our cone); a plan stating that FY2026 will land "at or above the top" of guidance (likely) or giving explicit FY2027 numbers (unlikely).

Versus the market. The market reads conservative guidance as a free option on upgrades. We read the same guidance as a sequence in which the upgrade comes last: a beat already banked, a first FY2027 range below consensus, then a raise in July 2027.

60

Score: 60. A four-year record of beating conservative guidance is top-quartile behaviour among European mid-caps; the absence of any mid-term frame, of guidance below EBITDA, and of any effort to hold consensus down, and a consensus that already sits above the range, pull the score to the upper-middle.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope and feedback loops

Judgement: Arteche demonstrated real pricing power in 2024-26 and has material operating leverage in both directions, but both depend on a regime of scarcity, and that regime has an end date. In FY2022-25 revenue growth produced outsized profit growth (EBITDA grew 4.6 times as fast as revenue) because price flowed through the direct margin. Over FY2025-30 EBITDA grows only about 1.4 times as fast as revenue, because the fixed cost base is being raised ahead of volume and price growth fades. Financial leverage is an option, not an amplifier; the scope to cut costs is small; and the reinforcing feedback loops dominate to FY2027, after which the balancing loops take over from FY2028.

Pricing power: Arteche raised prices faster than metal costs, but the gain is scarcity pricing, not structural pricing. The direct margin rose every year from FY2022 to H1 2026 while copper rose about 40% and steel about 34%. The chief financial officer ranks pricing first among H1 2026's drivers; industry prices rose 5% to 8% in the last year and 8% to 12% at high voltage; and volume discounts are trivial (€0.9m). Of the 6 points of direct margin gained since FY2020, about half is scarcity pricing and half is mix and efficiency (the SF6-free premium, now quoted at 10% to 15% against 20% to 30% earlier; lines above 245 kV; optical and automation products). The scarcity half, about 3 points, is what new industry capacity can take back.

Pricing durability varies by product. Pricing is strongest in high-voltage instrument transformers and inside the US fence; middling in relays; and weakest in medium voltage, in distribution (where R&S Group is destocking), and in Latin American and emerging-market tenders against Chinese and Indian bidders. The 2021-22 precedent is the reminder that Arteche's pricing depends on scarcity: under the same contract structures the direct margin fell 4.9 points, because indexation covers metals with a lag but not components, freight, energy or labour.

Operating leverage: the price lever is four times as powerful as the overhead lever, and the leverage is latent until volume catches up with the new fixed costs. In FY2025 purchases were about 50% of revenue, direct personnel 8.5%, direct operating expenses 4.9%, structural costs 22.3% and depreciation about 3%. The leverage is latent because capital spending (from €25m to about €43m), depreciation (from €15.9m to €24.5m by FY2028), overheads (23.9% of income in H1 2026) and SEG are all being added ahead of volume. The leverage turns positive if volume grows 12% to 15% a year, and negative if volume growth halves; Alfen's margin fall from 18% to 6% on falling volume against a fixed cost base shows what the negative case looks like.

Financial leverage: an option, not an amplifier. Net financial debt is €46m (0.5x EBITDA) on the company's basis, €79m including leases and about €125m including supplier finance. Interest on gross debt is only about €5m of the €9m net financial line; the rest (lease interest, factoring and guarantee costs, exchange differences, and hyperinflation adjustments in Turkey and Argentina) does not fall as net debt falls. Without acquisitions the balance sheet reaches net cash by FY2030, so the pressure is toward deals or a higher payout, not toward risk.

Cost-out: little scope, with one real lever. Procurement, lean manufacturing, product redesign and SEG purchasing save perhaps 1% to 2% of purchases a year, which offsets inflation (about 2.5% a year on an 82% cost base) rather than adding margin. In a downturn Arteche could remove costs worth 2 to 3 points of revenue within a year and 4 to 5 points over two years, slowly and expensively under Basque labour rules. The one real lever is overhead re-absorption: about 1.1 points of margin (€7m to €8m) by FY2028 if structural costs grow 11% and then 8% while revenue grows 14% and then 10.5%.

Feedback loops: the reinforcing loops carry Arteche to FY2027, and the balancing loops take over from FY2028. The scarcity-to-share loop (customers move volume to whoever can deliver, and Arteche added capacity ahead of rivals) has its own brake: backlog cover has lengthened from 7.4 to 9.4 months, so Arteche's delivery edge erodes unless the new plants ramp. On the balancing side, a bank withdrawing reverse-factoring lines would absorb about €34m of cash at once, as happened at Cembre in 2023; utilities face affordability limits, with European utility net debt up about 50% by 2030, Spanish allowed returns fixed to 2031 and Iberdrola re-pricing contracts at renewal. The capital-markets loop was reinforcing (a 201% share-price rise in 2025 funded the SEG purchase) and has now stalled, with the shares below the €33 placement price and more supply planned.

So what: the model's EBITDA margin path (18.0%, 18.4%, 18.6%, 18.5%, 18.3% for FY2026 to FY2030) is a forecast of pricing and mix first and of overheads second. The upside case for the multiple needs a positive price-cost spread beyond 2027, and the sector's history and the dated new capacity make that the less likely branch.

Strongest counter-case. Demand may absorb the new capacity (Bernstein, initiating on Pfisterer: "priced for a slowdown that isn't coming"), so that prices plateau at a high level and overhead re-absorption lifts the margin to 19.5% by FY2028. That is the model's upside case (EBITDA €153m, EPS €1.63), and it is a legitimate branch with about a 25% probability.

What would change my view. An H2 2026 margin at or above 18.5% (price-cost still positive); structural costs below 22.5% of income in H1 2027; or signs that the scarcity loop is stalling, such as new-order prices stabilising or falling in Europe, Tier-1 lead times shortening, or a book-to-bill ratio below 1.05.

Versus the market. The market extrapolates the H1 2026 margin as operating leverage still to come. We see the H1 2026 margin as price already delivered, with modest overhead leverage ahead and a tail of risk in both directions.

55

Score: 55. Demonstrated pricing power and a 2.2x degree of operating leverage put Arteche above the European median; the regime-dependence of the price, the fixed base rising ahead of volume, little cost-out scope and no structural scale economies keep it there rather than higher.

#6Forecast financials: double-digit growth, and higher growth and margins than the past

Judgement: the next four years look like a slower version of the last three, not a continuation. Revenue compounds at about 11% a year (near its own six-year rate), EBITDA at about 14% (against 47% in FY2022-25) and EPS at about 15% (against 80%), because the whole margin gain of the forecast period lands in FY2026 and the lines below EBIT normalise. Margins are far higher than in the past; growth is not. The FY2026 forecast is well founded and in line with consensus on EPS; the gap to consensus opens in FY2027 and widens in FY2028.

Below EBITDA: the lines that consensus under-models.

  • Depreciation rises from €18.3m to €29m, driven by capital spending of €43m to €45m a year in FY2026-27 and €40m to €42m after, and by five-year amortisation of about €7m a year of capitalised development.
  • Net financial items are €9m, easing to €7m.
  • The tax rate rises 17%, 19%, 20%, 21%, 22% over FY2026-30. Bizkaia's 24% nominal rate is cut by R&D deductions of €3.7m a year and a €15.1m deduction asset, and pushed up by Mexico at 30%, Brazil at 34%, Germany at about 30% and Bizkaia's new 19% minimum effective rate.
  • Minorities are €2.4m to €3.6m. SEG's acquisition amortisation of €1m to €2m a year from FY2027 is excluded from adjusted EPS.
  • Working capital is 19% of revenue to FY2027 and 18% by FY2030; the payout is 45%; net financial debt is about €50m at end-2026 and end-2027, turning to net cash by FY2030.

Against the past and the consensus: growth is similar to the past, the margin is higher, and the gap to consensus changes cause each year. Revenue grows 12.8% a year over FY2025-28, against 13.7% over FY2022-25; the EBITDA margin reaches 18.6% in FY2028, against 15.8% in FY2025; capital spending is 6% to 7.5% of revenue, against 4% to 6%; and free cash flow is 0.3x to 0.6x of net profit, against a fall from 1.8x to 0.6x. Against consensus, on the brokers' basis converted at the FY2025 gaps, Viewforth is below by 2%, 3% and 7% on revenue and by 3%, 5% and 10% on EBITDA for FY2026 to FY2028.

The cone of outcomes: FY2026 is almost closed, and consensus sits at or above the top of the cone for FY2027 and FY2028. For FY2026 the cone is EBITDA of €100m to €107m and EPS of €1.02 to €1.10. For FY2027 it is revenue of €621m to €684m, a margin of 17.0% to 19.0% and EPS of €0.98 to €1.37, with probabilities of 20% downside, 55% base and 25% upside (probability-weighted EPS about €1.21). For FY2028 the EPS cone is €0.87 to €1.63. The consensus means (€1.33 and €1.56) sit between our base and upside cases. The published means and medians imply that the unnamed third broker holds about €1.15 for FY2027 and €1.28 for FY2028, with margins near 17%; if so, the sell-side's own dispersion is as wide as our cone, and the median is simply Santander and JB Capital.

Two corrections to carry, neither large enough to change the forecast. First, SEG's pro-forma revenue (€9.9m for the five months to 11-Jun) puts its annual run-rate at €23m to €27m, not the model's €30m; the difference is half a point of FY2027 growth and under €1m of EBITDA, below the model's resolution. Second, the company does hedge transaction exposure (US dollar forwards of €45.6m notional) and has resumed commodity hedging, but the commodity notional is only €3.4m against roughly €17m a year of copper purchases, so the hedges only partly offset the copper-price lag assumed in the H2 2026 margin. I keep the 17.6% H2 2026 margin and note that the risk to it is upward.

So what: double-digit growth in revenue, EBITDA and EPS for four years is the base case, and after FY2026 that base is below what the market has written down. Around our base the skew is balanced for FY2026-27 and negative for FY2028-30; against consensus the skew is negative throughout.

Strongest counter-case. The model may be too cautious on three counts: on H2 2026 revenue (the backlog could support +21% if the plants ramp faster); on the H2 margin (the three-year pattern says 18.4% or more, and peer margins are still rising, with Končar at 21.2% and Schneider raising its range); and on tax (Santander's flat 16% has a year of evidence behind it). Each is possible, and together they make up the upside case. Even together they would lift FY2026 EPS only to about €1.10 to €1.13, in line with consensus.

What would change the numbers. H2 2026 revenue above €305m or below €285m; an H2 margin below 16.5% or above 18.5%; a 2030 margin ambition in the plan below 18% or at 20% or more; end-2026 working capital above 20% of revenue, or a fall in reverse factoring; the FY2026 tax rate and minorities in the March accounts.

Versus the market. We agree on FY2026. We are 8% to 13% below consensus on FY2027 EPS for reasons below EBIT, and 13% to 19% below on FY2028 EPS because of margin and revenue. We regard the single FY2029 estimate (€2.03) as one broker's, likely to be replaced by lower numbers as coverage widens.

62

Score: 62. Revenue, EBITDA and EPS compounding at 11% to 15% a year with margins near double their 2019-22 level is a top-third profile among European industrials; the deceleration from the recent past, the plateauing margin and the cash conversion keep it out of the top quartile.

#7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months

Judgement: the scope for upgrades is low. FY2026 will beat guidance but not consensus; the first FY2027 guidance is more likely to fall below consensus than above it; FY2027 and FY2028 consensus EPS are more likely to be cut than raised; and the Strategic Plan 2030 is more likely to be set to be beaten than to validate the bull broker. The upgrade cycle that lifted FY2027 EPS 34% in a year is over, and the next twelve months are about the market's numbers converging on ours.

The dated sequence: six events, most of them more likely to lower expectations than to raise them. The timeline below places each event; four points need more detail than the timeline carries.

  • The Strategic Plan 2030 could come any week, possibly after the 29-Nov election. We put about 70% on 2030 ambitions near our path (€845m to €950m of revenue, an 18% to 20% margin), 25% on ambitions near the bull broker's (€950m or more and 21%), and 20% on ambitions below €850m or below 18%. We put about 40% on a payout cut from 50% toward 30% to 45% to fund acquisitions, which domestic income holders would read badly and allocators well. An explicit FY2026 guidance raise at the plan is only 25% likely.
  • The Department of Energy rules (24-Dec-2026) are the positive novelty. The rules name Arteche's products and are likely to favour USMCA-compliant supply from Mexico.
  • The FY2026 results (24-Mar-2027) will show the tax rate, financial items, minorities and SEG's amortisation for the first time. These are the lines on which consensus is most exposed.
  • Coverage will widen with the float. International brokers initiating coverage tend to anchor on management's plan and a normalised tax rate, so the FY2027 consensus mean is likely to fall toward €1.25 to €1.30 while the buy share stays near 100%. That would be a consensus cut with no downgrade, and the dashboard's revision score would register it as negative momentum.

Upside triggers, listed honestly.

  • An H2 2026 margin at or above 18.4%, which would put FY2026 EBITDA at €106m or more and lift the FY2027 base.
  • A Strategic Plan 2030 at €950m of revenue and a 21% margin.
  • A bolt-on acquisition funded from the €150m to €250m of debt capacity (+5% to 7% of EPS per €100m spent).
  • Evidence that Hitachi Energy routes instrument-transformer or bushing volume to AGIT after GE Vernova's purchase of Trench.
  • Department of Energy rules that name Mexican assembly as compliant and lift US prices 3% to 5% (about +0.5 point on the group margin).
So what: for the next six months, monitor peers, regulators and markets rather than Arteche's own numbers, because Arteche reports twice a year and its one scheduled event with numbers is in March. Arteche's narrative is strongest now (the plan, the Department of Energy rules) and weakens through 2027 (Tier-1 capacity, the expiry of the 15% tariff rate on 31-Dec-2027, the margin-plateau debate), which is the opposite of the timing of the fundamentals.

Strongest counter-case. The plan may be the "beat and raise" that analysts expect, with 2030 targets of €1bn of revenue and a margin of 20% or more, resetting FY2027-29 consensus upward, while the Department of Energy rules and a strong H2 margin follow within three months. If all three land, FY2028 consensus holds and the multiple holds with it. I put that outcome at about one in four.

What would change my view. The plan's numbers; a third-quarter backlog figure; the H2 2026 margin.

Versus the market. The market's prevailing narrative is "beat and raise into a 2030 plan". Ours is "beat against guidance, guide below consensus, then raise": upgrades to guidance and downgrades to consensus, in that order.

34

Score: 34. With consensus already above guidance, estimates stalled at 0% over one month, a first FY2027 range likely below consensus and a plan likely to be set beatably, the scope for upgrades over the next six to twelve months is in the bottom third of European mid-caps despite a business that will deliver.

#8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and the same for peers

Judgement: Arteche's momentum is mixed and turning. Guidance momentum is positive but dated (July). Sell-side momentum is strong on a twelve-month view but has stopped (0% change in one month on EPS, EBITDA, sales and target price). Narrative momentum is positive but thin: two domestic brokers, 100% buy ratings and no investor commentary at all. Technical momentum is poor (the dashboard grades it D) despite a 12-month return of +80%. The peer group has de-rated hard around Arteche: the sector's relative strength fell from 69 to 14 in October, and the small-cap grid names are at the bottom of their valuation histories.

Evidence: the revisions have stopped, the price has fallen 17% from its high, and the technical pin is D. The buy share is 100%, up 33 points in three months. On 28-Oct-2026 the dashboard scored revision momentum at 10 and pinned sell-side earnings momentum at B, technical momentum at D and thematic fit at D. The shares fell about 17% from late September (€37.7) to late October while estimates did not move. Average daily value traded is about €1m. Co-movement with the peer basket is low (R-squared 5%, beta 0.45) but has risen in every window since March 2026.

Peers: the discount rate and positioning, not estimates, set the sector's share prices. The October sell-off hit Prysmian (−20%), Siemens Energy (−17%), ABB (−15%) and Legrand (−12%) even as Schneider raised guidance and ABB's orders rose 40%. On the dashboard, every one of the 16 sector peers carries technical momentum of D or worse except Landis+Gyr and Siemens (C). Three peers show what the small-cap grid band looks like after an order normalisation or a destocking: Pfisterer (graded F/D/A; P/E 14.1x at the 0th percentile; −21% over twelve months; orders −9% in H1 2026), R&S Group (D/F/B; 10.5x; −26%) and Kempower (F/F/A; −49%). The sector's valuation has split in two: quality compounders sit at high percentiles of their own histories (Siemens 98th, Landis+Gyr 95th, ABB 86th, Cembre 81st, Schneider 77th), and the small-cap grid and cable names sit at low ones (Pfisterer 0th, NKT 20th, Legrand 22nd, R&S 26th, Alfen 34th, Nexans 37th). Arteche, at the 91st percentile and 20.8x, sits with the first group, while its size, float and products belong with the second.

Inference: both patterns that lifted the stock are largely banked. The first pattern was the upgrade cycle (EPS rose 3.7 times from FY2023 to FY2025, and FY2027 consensus rose 34% in a year). The second was the small-cap re-rating (from about 10x in 2024 to over 20x, with a 470% share-price rise during the junior-market phase). The six- and twelve-month revision figures will decay mechanically as their windows roll forward, even if nobody cuts; by April 2027 the +18% six-month figure drops out. Technical momentum is already broken on the dashboard's rule while the price still sits just above a rising 200-day line, which is the pattern of a stock that has stopped going up but not yet started going down.

So what: momentum is not a reason to own the shares today, and the dashboard's pins (technical D, valuation F) say so. The sell-side B is the last of the three momentum measures to turn, and the dated events in #7 are the likely turning points.

Strongest counter-case. The sector's October de-rating may have been a positioning flush that reverses into year-end once the Federal Reserve's December rate rise is absorbed; Arteche's low beta protected it and may keep doing so; and a plan at the bull end could re-ignite the domestic narrative. That is plausible for weeks, not for the twelve-month horizon, because the widening float raises Arteche's co-movement with a cohort that has de-rated.

What would change my view. The price regaining and holding above the 50-day and 150-day averages (about €32 to €33) after the plan; a third-quarter trading update that restarts revisions; Pfisterer's third quarter showing orders re-accelerating, which would lift the whole small-cap grid band.

Versus the market. The domestic brokers' targets of €37 to €42 (mean €39.1, +25%) describe a stock with intact momentum. The dashboard's pins and the sector's October behaviour describe a stock whose momentum has stalled while its estimates have not yet been tested.

40

Score: 40. Strong twelve-month sell-side momentum and a rising 200-day line are offset by stalled revisions, a D technical pin, a 17% fall from the September high and a peer cohort at the bottom of its valuation history; the net is below the European median.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Judgement: the fundamental case is simple and monitorable; the share-price case is fragile. Two drivers (the direct margin and the capacity ramp) explain the difference between the next four years and the last six; both are reported half-yearly; and the FY2026-27 cone is narrow on revenue and EBITDA. The fragility has three sources: both drivers depend on the same regime of scarcity; the earnings line carries three lines that no one guides; and the shares trade on a multiple at the top of their history, with a thin and expanding float, two brokers, and a peer precedent of a 48% fall on a positioning unwind. The sector's own history says share prices turn on the rate of change of orders, well before margins peak.

Simplicity: two signals explain the forecast, and the half-to-half swings are noise around them. One line, the direct margin, explains all of the difference in profitability: each point is worth about €6.6m of EBITDA, and each 1% of price about 0.8 point of margin. One driver, converting a nine-month backlog through four new plants, explains the revenue path. Three mechanical lines (the tax rate rising from 14% to 22%, depreciation rising €13m by FY2030, and minorities) explain why EPS growth converges on EBITDA growth. The half-to-half noise is real: revenue growth by half has swung between +4% and +24% over five years, and Latin American revenue fell 8.6% in H1 2026 on the timing of recloser orders. That noise surrounds two signals; it is not a third signal.

Fragilities and assumptions: seven things must hold.

  1. Prices hold through FY2027, which depends on scarcity persisting.
  2. Overheads re-absorb, from 23.9% to 22.4% of income.
  3. Three plants and the Mexican expansion ramp at once; the peer base rate is a 12-to-18-month ramp with a temporary drag of 100 to 150 basis points.
  4. SEG delivers its first full year, although a 5-point margin miss at SEG costs the group only 0.25 point.
  5. Working capital normalises; Arteche has not yet shown it, and peers took 12 to 18 months.
  6. The reverse-factoring lines stay in place.
  7. The tax rate rises no faster than modelled.

Sudden, high-magnitude risks: the fundamental risks are not existential, but a 20% to 35% fall in a risk-off quarter needs no change in fundamentals. Among the fundamental risks, US trade treatment of Mexican-made equipment matters most because North America is about 29% to 33% of revenue. The product-failure precedents are Alfen's €15.4m Pacto provision and Arteche's own €1.4m provision for Brazilian reclosers. The largest client, Mexico's state utility CFE (Comisión Federal de Electricidad), is about 14% of revenue. Among the perception-driven risks, a family placement into a weak market would meet June's buyers at €33 already under water, and the debate over financing artificial-intelligence data centres hangs over anything traded as a grid-for-data-centres name.

Trackability: good on the operating lines, poor in frequency. Orders, backlog, the direct margin, structural costs, working capital and factoring balances are all disclosed half-yearly. Arteche publishes no quarterly profit and loss, segment EBITDA only annually, no split of price, volume and mix, no standalone SEG figures, no guidance below EBITDA and no hedge coverage ratios. Over the next six months investors will see Pfisterer's third quarter, Siemens Energy's capital markets day (11-Nov-2026), Hammond's and Končar's quarterly results and the Department of Energy rules before Arteche says anything with numbers.

Sector and cyclical precedents: grid-equipment booms end in overcapacity, and Arteche shares the 2026 template but not yet the trigger. Transmission downcycles have run for up to seven years. Arteche itself ran EBITDA margins of 7.5% to 10.9% through 2022. Arteche's orders are still growing 15.7%, so the 2026 trigger (Pfisterer's orders fell 9% against an exceptional 2025; R&S Group suffered distribution destocking, installer bottlenecks and a plant ramp; Alfen's adjacency commoditised) has not arrived.

Two rules of thumb from the sector are worth carrying. The first: "the first half of a one-to-two-year holding is the cleaner half, before the market debates the plateau after 2028". The second, "a price plateau at a high level is two to three more years of rising margin", holds for cable makers with five-year backlogs, but not for Arteche's nine-month backlog.

So what: separate the sources of any miss, and size the position for a drawdown unrelated to the numbers. Judge Arteche's delivery on revenue, direct margin, structural costs and EBITDA; judge consensus risk on the four lines below EBIT; and do not attribute an earnings miss to operations until the two have been separated. Size the position for a 30% drawdown that has nothing to do with the numbers.

Strongest counter-case. The fundamental simplicity may be the point: a nine-month backlog, a 20% capacity addition, a 40% direct margin and 0.5x leverage make Arteche one of the most forecastable mid-caps in the sector, and the share-price fragility is then a reason to buy the dips rather than avoid the name. I agree with the first half of that argument; the second half depends on the entry multiple (#11).

What would change my view. Quarterly reporting or a third-quarter trading figure (raises trackability); a third broker from a bulge-bracket house (lowers the risk of a single downgrade); the float reaching 25% (lowers placement risk, but raises co-movement with the sector).

Versus the market. The market treats the case as simple in both dimensions: a grid-supercycle compounder on a quality multiple. We treat it as simple fundamentally and fragile in price, and we think the price dimension decides the next twelve months.

42

Score: 42. Two observable drivers, a narrow FY2026-27 operating cone and a strong balance sheet make the business less risky than most European industrials; a regime-dependent margin, half-yearly disclosure, three ungauged earnings lines and a share-price setup that matches the sector's worst 2026 precedent make the expectations riskier than most, and the net sits below the median.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Judgement: Arteche is in late Broadening, with the leading indicators of Stalling already present. The thesis broadened in 2025-26 (the main-market listing, the wider float, SEG, the automation pivot, the US fence, Capital Research's stake), and delivery is at its peak (record orders and margin, and a guidance raise). But the upgrade engine has stopped (0% in one month), technical momentum has turned (D), the multiple is at the 91st percentile, the fundamental peers have already moved to Stalling or Collapsing, and the next dated guidance event is more likely negative than positive. The dashboard's rule puts the starting phase at Broadening; I would describe it as the last stage of Broadening, where the fundamentals still reinforce the thesis and the share price has begun to stall.

Evidence by lens: three lenses point to Stalling, and only the fundamentals still improve.

LensReading
MomentumSell-side B but flat; technical D; price −17% from the September high while estimates held
Scope for upgradesLow over 6 to 12 months (#7)
Risk factorsValuation at the top of its range, supply from the family, two brokers, a peer precedent
FundamentalsStill improving (orders, backlog, margin), with the plateau dated to FY2027-28

Inference: the stock already trades as if the pricing peak will not come, while every broker who has studied the sector dates it to 2026-27. The sequence the sector's history describes runs in three steps: share prices peak around the time order growth peaks; executed margins lag new-order pricing by one to three years; and the market debates the plateau long before reported margins turn. Arteche's order growth has not yet peaked (orders +15.7%). The convergence risk is toward the small-cap grid band (Pfisterer, R&S and Alfen at 10x to 14x), not away from it, and the widening float accelerates the convergence.

So what: a stock moving from Broadening to Stalling on a peak multiple is the setup Richard's framework treats most cautiously, because the forecasts are more uncertain than the delivery record suggests and the multiple has no cushion. The constructive reading is that Arteche may complete a mini-cycle inside eighteen months: Stalling through the March 2027 guidance and a placement, then Turning Up on the H1 2027 raise and the first evidence that the 2030 plan is being beaten, at a multiple two to four turns lower. That lower multiple is the entry the business deserves.

Strongest counter-case. Arteche may be in early Broadening, not late: the main-market listing is nine months old; index inclusion (IBEX Medium Cap, MSCI small cap, STOXX) is still ahead and would bring passive demand once the float reaches 20% to 25%; international coverage has not started; and the plan will reset the narrative upward. All of that is true, and all of it supports the current multiple rather than adding to it, because the liquidity discount these events were meant to remove has already left the price.

What would change my view. A plan at the bull end plus a strong H2 margin (the stock would stay in Broadening); a third-quarter order figure below 10% growth in constant currency (the stock would move straight to Stalling on fundamentals, not just on price); a placement absorbed at a small discount by new institutional holders (lowers the supply risk).

Versus the market. The market (two domestic brokers, 100% buy ratings, targets +25%) sees a stock in the Reinforcing phase. We see Broadening with a Stalling share price, and we think the next six months are more likely to confirm our reading than the market's.

38

Score: 38. Peak delivery and a broadened thesis argue for the upper half; stalled revisions, a D technical pin, a peak multiple and a cohort already in Stalling or Collapsing put the phase judgement below the median of European stocks on attractiveness.

#11The fair multiple

Judgement: Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Broadening stock is the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history of two-year-forward P/E, which for Arteche is 17.67x. That is 25% below the 23.4x the model computes on its own earnings (19.8x on consensus; 20.8x on current-year earnings, at the 91st percentile). I accept 17.67x as fair, regard it as generous rather than mean for three reasons, and see the skew around it as downward.

Reason 1: the history is short and belongs to a different company. Arteche has 48 months of P/E data since November 2021, most of them as a junior-market micro-cap trading at 10x to 14x on single-digit margins. The ten-year median is 13.6x, the 75th percentile 16.8x and the 90th percentile 20.3x. The 80th percentile of that history therefore applies a main-market premium to a junior-market distribution.

Reason 2: the fundamental peers trade far below 17.67x. Pfisterer trades at 14.1x (the 0th percentile of its history), R&S at 10.5x, Nexans at 11.5x and NKT at 15.7x. The Trench transaction, the best private-market reference for the niche, was struck at 13x 2028 EBITDA (18x 2026). At 10x FY2027 consensus EBITDA, Arteche's equity is worth about €20 a share.

Reason 3: the business is entering a margin plateau with decelerating EPS growth. EPS growth slows to 11% in FY2028, then 8% and 7%. The reinvestment runway (about 8% to 10% of sales reinvested at high returns, bounded by the capacity cycle) supports a mid-cycle multiple in the mid-to-high teens, not the 20x to 30x the shares have carried since the listing.

Why not lower: the quality is real, and the fair multiple follows the margin path the company proves. The quality is real and improving: a top-two niche position, 18% margins that Pfisterer's and Trench's economics say belong to the niche, 0.5x leverage, a four-year record of beats and a 45% to 50% payout. The stock's price movements are 95% idiosyncratic today, so sector rotation does not drive it day to day. The stock will also carry some scarcity premium as the only listed Spanish grid-equipment company while its float, coverage and index inclusion broaden.

The dashboard's pins disagree, and the F is the honest one. The dashboard rates valuation F (P/E at the 91st percentile of ten years) and total shareholder return / valuation C. The C was re-based from the September memo's higher return estimate, and the dashboard notes that the pin and the re-based return disagree by two grades or more. The F is the honest reading of today's price.

So what: the de-rating from 23.4x to 17.67x is a 25% headwind that earnings growth of about 21% over fourteen months does not fully offset, and on after-minorities earnings the headwind is about 4% larger. The multiple is the dominant lever in the total-return arithmetic of #12.

Strongest counter-case. The sector's quality compounders (Schneider 21.3x, ABB 21.2x, Siemens 19.1x, Cembre 19.7x) may be the right reference for a top-two niche leader with Arteche's growth, which would make 20x to 22x fair for a Broadening stock. That is the market's implicit view, and it requires the margin path the bull broker has written down.

What would change my view. A plan at €950m and 21% with a credible bridge (raises the fair band to 19x to 21x); international initiations at normalised numbers (confirms the band); the first FY2027 guidance below consensus (lowers the market's multiple toward ours, which is the entry event).

Versus the market. The market pays 20x to 23x for the consensus path. We would pay 17.67x for our path, and we think the market will be paying something close to 17.67x within twelve months.

28

Score: 28. A guideline fair multiple 25% below the current one, a current P/E at the 91st percentile of its own history and a cohort at the 0th to 37th place Arteche in the bottom third of European stocks on the attractiveness of its multiple today, even though the business merits the upper half of the sector's range.

#12Total shareholder return, via the Dupont split

Judgement: at the guideline multiple the total shareholder return is negative to end-2027 and about nil to mid-2029. Earnings do their job (+21.5% and +40.7%), the de-rating undoes it (−29.5% and −32.3%), and dividends add 3.3% and 5.2%. The arithmetic is simple, and the lever is the multiple.

The model's figures (price €31.40; two-year-forward P/E now 23.4x; the guideline 17.67x reached at the 18-month column).

HorizonTotal shareholder returnAnnualisedValue per shareFrom dividendsFrom the multipleFrom earnings
To 31-Dec-2027 (about 14 months)−11.1%−9.5%€27.93+3.3%−29.5%+21.5%
To 30-Jun-2029 (about 32 months)+0.4%+0.2%€31.53+5.2%−32.3%+40.7%

How to read the 18-month figure: the earnings base rolls forward while the multiple falls. Today's 23.4x is the price divided by the average of FY2027 and FY2028 model EPS (€1.34). By end-2027 the forward base rolls to FY2029 EPS of €1.52, and that roll is the +21.5% from earnings. At 17.67x, €1.52 of EPS is worth €26.9 a share; adding about €1.0 of dividends (€0.48 for FY2026 and €0.55 for FY2027) gives €27.9 in all, 11% below today's price. The three-year figure rolls the base to a FY2030-31 blend of about €1.69, worth about €30 at 17.67x, plus about €1.6 of dividends. On after-minorities earnings (€1.47 and about €1.62, instead of €1.52 and €1.69) each return is about 4 points lower: roughly −14% and −4%.

What drives the return, and what moves it.

  • Earnings. The +21.5% is the model's FY2027-29 EPS growth (+15%, +11%, +8%). The consensus path (FY2029 EPS of €2.03) would make it +51%, and the downside path (FY2028 EPS of €0.87) about −35%.
  • The multiple. Each turn is worth 4.8% of today's price (Judgement 4 in #0). Breaking even at end-2027 needs about 20x on our earnings, while the consensus path at 17.67x would give about +17%. The whole bull case is therefore the gap between €1.52 and €2.03 of FY2029 EPS.
  • Dividends. A 45% payout on growing earnings gives a 1.5% to 2% yield, which is immaterial to the result.
  • Cash returns beyond dividends. There are none: Arteche has never bought back shares, and the balance sheet's spare capacity is more likely to fund acquisitions (+5% to 7% of EPS per €100m) than returns to shareholders.
So what: the shares are priced for the consensus path at a quality-compounder multiple. The distribution of returns over the next 6 to 18 months is skewed negative. Over three years the distribution is roughly balanced around zero with fat tails on both sides, and the right tail (the plan, acquisitions, the US fence) is as real as the left tail (the capacity wave, the placement, guidance below consensus).

Strongest counter-case. The multiple may not de-rate, because the business keeps delivering, coverage broadens with buy ratings, index inclusion brings passive demand and the plan is strong. In that world the return to end-2027 is the earnings growth plus the yield, about +20% to +25%, which matches the brokers' targets of €37 to €42. That world requires the market to keep paying 23x for a margin plateau, which the market has not done this year for any of Arteche's fundamental peers.

What would change my view. A de-rating event (the March guidance or a placement) that brings the price toward €24 to €27 (16x to 18x FY2029 earnings) without a change in our numbers. At that price the same Dupont split gives +10% to +15% a year to mid-2029 on our path and much more on the consensus path, and the case flips from "wait" to "act".

Versus the market. The brokers' targets imply +18% to +35% over twelve months at an unchanged multiple. We get −11% to end-2027 at the guideline multiple and about nil to mid-2029. The difference is entirely the multiple and the FY2028-29 margin.

22

Score: 22. A negative total return over the next 14 months and roughly nil over three years at the guideline multiple put Arteche in the bottom quarter of European stocks on prospective return, despite earnings growth that would, on its own, rank in the top third.

#13Summary conclusion

Arteche is a high-quality, well-run specialist in the right place at the right time. Arteche holds a top-two position in a niche gated by utility homologation; its demand environment moved from planned to legally funded in the last six months; a US regulatory fence now surrounds its products; its record backlog makes revenue a question of conversion rather than demand; and its management sets guidance low and beats it every year. On the fundamentals, the next eighteen months are among the most predictable in the sector: revenue growth of 13% to 14%, an EBITDA margin held at 18% or better, and EPS after minorities of €1.06 in FY2026 and about €1.22 in FY2027.

The investment case over the next 6 to 18 months is weak, because the share price already contains a better version of Arteche's story than the one we can support. The margin step is in the accounts and came from price, not operating leverage; from FY2027 the margin plateaus; the lines below EBIT normalise in ways the two domestic brokers have not modelled; the first FY2027 guidance will most likely land below consensus; the family will sell more stock; and the multiple sits at the 91st percentile of its history while every fundamental peer has already de-rated to the low teens. At the guideline fair multiple the model returns −11% to end-2027 and about nil to mid-2029, and in the short run the skew around those returns is downward.

The case over three years is interesting, because the de-rating is likely to be dated and visible, and the business on the other side of it compounds. After the de-rating Richard would own a business that compounds revenue at 8% to 10% a year, pays out 45% of earnings, carries €150m to €250m of acquisition capacity and benefits from regulatory fences that strengthen over time. The practical conclusion is to want this stock, but not at this price: let the sequence of events in #7 run, watch the direct margin and the structural-cost ratio each half-year, and look to re-engage after the March 2027 guidance or the next placement, once the market has learned how Arteche guides and the multiple has moved toward that of Arteche's own cohort.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: B. Funded, dated external mandates and a US fence, plus a broad internal programme of capacity, acquisitions and listing, rank in the top quarter of European companies; the forces are a response to the cycle rather than a transformation, and the price component of the external force has peaked.

Foundations' Robustness: B. A homologation-gated top-two niche position, 18% margins the niche's economics support, 0.5x leverage and a four-year delivery record are top-quarter foundations; cash conversion, half-yearly disclosure and governance at regulatory minimums stop it short of an A.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. The business fits Viewforth's Demand-driven EPSU (earnings step-up) setup, but the step-up has already happened and is in consensus; there is no cause for concern to clear and no rebase to revert from; and the acquisitions are too few and too small for the Serial Acquirer setup. The setup would re-form crisply as a Demand-driven EPSU on a second-quartile (Q2) multiple after a de-rating event in 2027.

Case Riskiness: C. The operating case is simple, concentrated in two observable drivers and low-risk for 18 months; the earnings line carries three ungauged items and the share price carries a peak multiple, a thin expanding float, two brokers and the sector's worst 2026 precedent, which together make the expectations case average-risk rather than simple.
